title: the summit sit
hook: a weaver, a tailor, a shopkeeper and a princess, all singing to God in the language of home
carry: say one kind thing in your first language

segments.voice: Yesterday the summit sit went back to Krishna's childhood, and Yashoda saw the universe and was given back her son. Did you come back to something small and near? Today, the singers. Day one thousand forty-nine.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `VAST, AND SMALL, AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: A weaver at his loom in Varanasi, throwing the shuttle and singing. A tailor in Maharashtra with a needle in his hand and a name of God on his lips. A shopkeeper whose ledgers of money owed to him, the story goes, ended up in the river. A princess in Rajasthan who sang that she had no one but Krishna. A girl in a Tamil temple town who wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered. Those are some of the faces from the weeks of the saints of bhakti. Today's summit sit climbs back to them.
screen: `A WEAVER, A TAILOR, A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A PRINCESS, A GARDEN GIRL.` → `THE SAINTS OF BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: From the top of the year, look at who the tradition chose to remember. Kabir is remembered as a weaver. Namdev as a tailor. Tukaram as a small trader whose business failed. Mirabai as a princess who walked away from palace rules. Andal as a girl raised by a temple gardener. Looms, needles, ledgers, a palace, a garden. They're remembered for what they sang. And notice what they sang in. Andal and the Nayanars sang in Tamil. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram in Marathi. Kabir, Surdas, Tulsidas and Mirabai in the spoken tongues of the north. In Bengal, the songs of Chaitanya's kirtan were made in Bengali. The language of the kitchen and the market became a language of prayer. Listen to the kind of thing they said. A song credited to Kabir lets God speak, in paraphrase: where are you looking for me? I am right beside you. Not in the temple, not in the mosque, not in ritual and renunciation. Seek truly and you will find me in a moment. Mirabai, in paraphrase: my own is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. Different saints, different gods named, different tongues. One shared move: love spoken plainly, by whoever you happen to be, wherever you happen to stand. Songs from those weeks are still sung by heart in kitchens, on pilgrim roads, and in temple halls.
screen: `REMEMBERED BY THEIR TRADES.` · `SUNG IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `I AM RIGHT BESIDE YOU.` · `NO ONE ELSE BUT GIRIDHAR GOPAL.` · then, large: `LOVE, SPOKEN PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Sit for the bell's two minutes. Find the language you first heard tenderness in, whatever it is. If you pray, you can let one name of God, in that language, rest on the breath, quietly, again and again, the way the saints repeated a name. If you don't, choose a plain word for thanks in that same tongue. No need to say it aloud. Let it come and go with the breath, like a weaver's shuttle, back and forth. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Loving devotion, the saints' whole path, sung to God in the language of home.

Your line: say one kind thing in your first language. Today, say one kind thing in the language you grew up with, to someone who will understand it, or quietly to yourself. Day one thousand forty-nine.

howItsDone: The songs of the bhakti saints are sung in homes, temples and on pilgrim walks across India: Tukaram's abhangas, Kabir's dohas, Mirabai's bhajans and Andal's Tiruppavai, each in its own language.

fork.setup: a seeker asks where to look for God: in the temple, on pilgrimage, or in rituals. what does Kabir's song say?
options: in the great temple, at the right hour.
on a long pilgrimage, far from home.
right beside you, if you truly seek.
fork.reveal: the song turns the question around: not in temple or mosque or ritual, but right beside the seeker, found in a moment of true seeking.

notes: Third summit sit (1047–1053): revisits the saints of bhakti block (907–936).

Hagiographical details are framed as how the saints are remembered: Kabir a weaver of Varanasi; Namdev a tailor; Tukaram a trader whose business failed and whose debt deeds went into the Indrayani ('the story goes'); Mirabai a Rajput princess; Andal raised by Periyalvar, a temple garland-maker, who wore the god's garland first. Check each, including 'Andal ... dressed in the garland meant for the god' and 'raised by a temple gardener'.

Language attributions: Andal and Nayanars Tamil; Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Tukaram Marathi; Kabir, Surdas, Tulsidas, Mirabai northern vernaculars (Braj, Awadhi, Rajasthani); Chaitanya's kirtan in Bengali. Confirm.

Kabir paraphrase draws on Songs of Kabir I (Tagore 1915, public domain but not on the validator's list); it mentions temple and mosque as Kabir does. Mirabai paraphrase of 'mere to giridhar gopal, dusro na koi'.
The teach lists the five by trade or station (looms, needles, ledgers, a palace, a garden) without ranking them; confirm the framing.

Editor pass: fixed the garbled Tukaram line (the ledgers in the river were debts owed to him); Andal 'wore' the garland; Chaitanya line no longer implies kirtan was wholly Bengali; the Kabir paraphrase now says God is the speaker, as in the song; fork no longer casts the listener as Kabir.
Audit 2026-10-01: checked the Kabir paraphrase against Songs of Kabir I and the trade and language attributions; no change.
